name: Vinaceous-Cinnamon
lede: Vinaceous-Cinnamon is a warm, wine-tinged orange-brown, a deeper member of Robert Ridgway's "vinaceous" family carried over from his 1886 bird-and-mammal nomenclature.

sections.title: Cinnamon with a wine cast
sections.body:
Ridgway first used this name in 1886 and replated it in 1912 at plate XXIX, hue 13'', tone b [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[pinkish-cinnamon]], [[onion-skin-pink]], [[antique-brass]] and [[apricot-buff]], at 3.3, 3.3, 3.9 and 4.3 ΔE [1]. The ISCC-NBS system later filed it as block 29, a moderate orange [1].

In our library it is an exact color match to [[light-cinnamon]] (CIEDE2000 0.0), and its nearest distinct neighbors are [[pinkish-cinnamon]] and [[onion-skin-pink]], both within 3.3 units [2]. Measured in LCH it is lightness 68, chroma 34 and hue 57 degrees, noticeably more saturated than its paler sibling Vinaceous-Buff [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this orange-brown in 696 of 23,781 paintings (2.93%, as photographed), more common than 80% of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in paintings from the 1500s, at 2.1 times the expected rate for that century, and most often plays an accent, in 52% of its 395 strongest matches [3]. Pontormo is its most devoted painter, at 5.3 times the baseline rate across his 13 works here [3]. It is also most over-represented in paintings from India, at 2.7 times the expected rate [3]. The earliest dated match runs to the year 1000, long before Ridgway's 1886 record; the match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof the pigment was there, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3].

origin.source: Ridgway, Color Standards and Color Nomenclature (1912), carried over from 1886
